title: Hernán Cortés
subtitle: The conquistador who brought down the Aztec Empire

package.intro: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with about five hundred soldiers. Two years later, Tenochtitlan, one of the largest cities in the world, lay in ruins. This documentary tells how it happened, and why the old story of a few hundred conquerors leaves most of it out.
facts: Born in 1485 in Medellín, Extremadura, Spain
Sailed from Cuba in February 1519 with 11 ships, about 500 soldiers and 16 horses
Entered Tenochtitlan and met Moctezuma II on 8 November 1519
The Spaniards fled the city on La Noche Triste, the night of 30 June to 1 July 1520
A smallpox epidemic in 1520 killed Moctezuma's successor, Cuitláhuac
Tenochtitlan fell and Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521
Made Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca in 1529
Died at Castilleja de la Cuesta, near Seville, on 2 December 1547
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bernal Díaz del Castillo's True History of the Conquest of New Spain, the Florentine Codex, Matthew Restall's When Montezuma Met Cortés and Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest, Hugh Thomas's The Conquest of Mexico.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: HERNÁN CORTÉS
lines.sub: The conquistador who brought down the Aztec Empire

lines: On the eighth of November 1519, a few hundred Spanish soldiers marched along a causeway across a lake into Tenochtitlan, one of the largest cities on Earth. Their commander was met by the emperor himself.
Historians estimate the city held perhaps two hundred thousand people, far more than any city in Spain. Less than two years later, it lay in ruins.

lines.label: Spanish soldiers who sailed with Cortés in 1519

lines: Hernán Cortés had set out with about five hundred soldiers. The empire he brought down ruled millions of people.

lines.text: How did a few hundred men topple an empire?

lines: The real answer is not the old story of a handful of heroes and their guns. It involves an epidemic, tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, and a man prepared to do almost anything to win.

sections.name: A restless young man
lines: Hernán Cortés was born in 1485 in Medellín, in western Spain, to a family of minor nobility with little money.
At nineteen he sailed for Hispaniola, the island colony founded by Columbus. In 1511 he joined the conquest of Cuba under its new governor, Diego Velázquez.

lines.name: Hernán Cortés
lines.role: Minor noble from Extremadura. Landowner and official in Cuba.

lines: In Cuba he became a landowner and official, known for his charm and ambition. He fell in and out of favour with Velázquez more than once.
In 1518 Velázquez chose him to lead an expedition to the newly sighted coast of Mexico, to explore and trade. Then he changed his mind. Cortés sailed anyway.

sections.name: Landing
lines: He left Cuba in February 1519 with eleven ships, about five hundred soldiers, sixteen horses and a handful of cannon.
On the island of Cozumel he found Gerónimo de Aguilar, a Spaniard shipwrecked years earlier, who had learned to speak Maya.

lines.name: Malintzin
lines.role: Enslaved Nahua woman given to Cortés. Spoke Nahuatl and Maya.

lines: After defeating a Maya army on the coast, Cortés was given twenty enslaved women. One, Malintzin, spoke Maya and Nahuatl, the language of the Aztec Empire. She became his interpreter, adviser, and later the mother of his son.

lines.title: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz

lines: Then he made a legal move. His men founded a town, Veracruz, whose council named him its captain, answerable to the king rather than to Velázquez.

lines.text: He did not burn his ships. He wrecked them.

lines: To stop supporters of Velázquez from turning back, he had his ships run aground and wrecked. The famous story that he burned them is a later embellishment.

sections.name: Allies
lines: The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three cities, dominated by the Mexica of Tenochtitlan. It took tribute from dozens of subject peoples, many of whom resented it. Some neighbours, like Tlaxcala, had never been conquered.
The emperor's envoys brought gifts of gold, hoping to keep the strangers away. It had the opposite effect.
Cortés exploited the empire's divisions. The Totonacs of the coast joined him. The Tlaxcalans fought him first, then became his most important allies.

At Cholula, a city allied to the Aztecs, Cortés claimed to have uncovered a plot against him. His men and their allies killed several thousand of its people. Whether there really was a plot is still disputed.

sections.name: Tenochtitlan

lines.label: Tenochtitlan · the city on the lake

lines: Tenochtitlan stood on islands in a lake, linked to the shore by causeways, with great markets, temples and canals. The Spaniards had never seen anything like it.
On the eighth of November 1519, Cortés met the emperor, Moctezuma the Second, on the causeway. Moctezuma welcomed the Spaniards and lodged them in a palace.

lines.name: Moctezuma II
lines.role: Ruler of the Mexica and the Aztec Empire from 1502.

lines: Why he let them in is debated. A popular story says he took Cortés for a returning god. Many historians now doubt it, and think the story was invented after the conquest.
Within about a week, Cortés took Moctezuma hostage in his own city, and began to rule through him.
In 1520 Velázquez sent a larger force to arrest Cortés. Cortés marched to the coast, defeated it in a night attack, and recruited most of its men.
While he was away, his deputy, Pedro de Alvarado, attacked Mexica nobles during a religious festival at the city's great temple, killing many of them. The city rose against the Spaniards.

lines.text: How Moctezuma died is still disputed.

lines: Cortés returned to find his men besieged, and Moctezuma died within weeks. Spanish accounts say his own people stoned him as he appealed for calm. Indigenous accounts say the Spaniards killed him.

sections.name: The Sad Night
lines: On the night of the thirtieth of June 1520, the Spaniards tried to escape across a causeway and were caught. Hundreds of Spaniards and many more of their allies died. They called it La Noche Triste, the Sad Night.
Days later, the exhausted survivors won a desperate battle at Otumba and reached safety in Tlaxcala.

Then came something no one had planned. Smallpox, brought to Mexico with the Spanish reinforcements, spread through a population with no immunity. It killed huge numbers, including Moctezuma's successor, Cuitláhuac.

sections.name: The fall of the city
lines: Cortés rebuilt his army in Tlaxcala. He had thirteen small warships built, carried in pieces overland, and launched on the lake around the city.

lines.label: Indigenous allies in the siege of 1521

lines: The siege began in May 1521. About a thousand Spaniards took part. Beside them fought tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all Tlaxcalans, who did most of the fighting.

Starving and ravaged by disease, the defenders held out for nearly three months as the attackers destroyed the city street by street. On the thirteenth of August 1521, the last emperor, Cuauhtémoc, was captured.
Estimates of the dead in the siege run from tens of thousands to well over a hundred thousand. Many died of hunger and disease.

sections.name: The reward
lines: Cuauhtémoc was tortured to reveal where the city's gold was hidden. Little was found. In 1525, on an expedition to Honduras, Cortés had him hanged on suspicion of plotting.
Emperor Charles the Fifth made Cortés governor of the new colony of New Spain. Mexico City rose on the ruins of Tenochtitlan.
The conquerors were rewarded with encomiendas, grants of Indigenous people who had to work for them and pay them tribute. Cortés himself was later granted some twenty-three thousand vassals.

Over the next century, waves of epidemics, combined with forced labour and upheaval, caused central Mexico's population to collapse. Many historians estimate it fell by as much as ninety percent, though the starting figure is fiercely debated.
Cortés's power faded. Rivals accused him of misrule, and the crown sent officials to rein him in. He was made a marquis, rich, but never again trusted with real power.

lines.name: Marquis of the Valley
lines.role: Rich, titled, and sidelined by the crown he had enriched.

lines: He led an expedition to Baja California, then returned to Spain to press his claims at court. He died near Seville in December 1547, still petitioning the king.

sections.name: Legacy

lines.text: The conquest was also an Indigenous war.

lines: Historians such as Matthew Restall have challenged the old story of a few hundred Spaniards defeating an empire. It was also a revolt by peoples the Aztecs had dominated, who did most of the fighting and dying.
Smallpox, steel, horses and Cortés's own nerve all mattered. But his allies were soon disappointed. The Tlaxcalans kept some privileges, yet they too ended up under Spanish rule.
In Mexico he is remembered mostly as a destroyer. In 2019, Mexico's president asked Spain's king to apologise for the conquest. The Spanish government rejected the request.

Malintzin's memory is contested too. For generations, malinchista was an insult for someone who sides with foreigners against their own people. Many now see her as an enslaved young woman who survived the only way she could.

Cortés did not conquer Mexico alone. But he saw how to turn an empire's enemies, and an epidemic, into weapons, and he never hesitated to use them. A great city, and a whole world, ended because of it.
